sections.title: Present Simple vs Continuous
sections.rule: Use the present simple for habits, routines, and permanent facts: subject + base verb (add -s for he/she/it). Use the present continuous (am/is/are + verb-ing) for actions happening right now or temporary situations. Stative verbs like know, want, and like normally stay simple even when we mean 'now'.
sections.example_target: I work in a bank, but this week I am working from home.
sections.example_target_2: She usually walks, but today she is driving.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'work' is her permanent job (habit); 'am working from home' is temporary and true only now. / 'walks' is her routine; 'is driving' is happening today only.
sections.note: Never say 'I am knowing' or 'I am wanting' — state verbs (know, want, like, believe, understand) stay in the simple form.

sections.title: Past Simple vs Present Perfect
sections.rule: Use the past simple for finished actions at a specific past time (yesterday, in 2019, last week). Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) for past actions with a present connection or an unspecified time. Pair the present perfect with since, for, just, already, ever, and yet.
sections.example_target: I visited Rome in 2019, and I have already been there three times.
sections.example_target_2: She has just finished her homework.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'visited' names a finished time (2019); 'have been' counts experience up to now with no exact date. / 'has just finished' = completed a moment ago, still relevant now.
sections.note: A specific past time (yesterday, last year) forces the past simple. You cannot say 'I have seen him yesterday' — say 'I saw him yesterday'.

sections.title: Future: Will vs Going To
sections.rule: Use 'will' for spontaneous decisions, predictions, offers, and promises. Use 'going to' for plans decided before speaking or predictions based on present evidence. Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements with a time and place.
sections.example_target: I think it will rain, and look at those clouds — it is going to pour.
sections.example_target_2: I am meeting Sam at six tonight.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'will rain' is a general prediction; 'going to pour' is based on the clouds you can see now. / 'am meeting' is a fixed arrangement (time and person already set).
sections.note: Decide as you speak (offering help, reacting) = will. Already planned or clear evidence = going to. Fixed appointment = present continuous.

sections.title: Modal Verbs
sections.rule: Modals (can, could, must, have to, should, might, may, would) come before the base verb with no 'to' and no -s: 'She can swim', not 'She cans'. They express ability, obligation, advice, possibility, and politeness. 'Have to' is the exception — it changes form (has to) and uses do/does in questions and negatives.
sections.example_target: You must wear a helmet, but you don't have to buy a new one.
sections.example_target_2: She might come, and you should ask her.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'must' = strong obligation; 'don't have to' = it is not necessary (no obligation). / 'might come' = possibility; 'should ask' = advice.
sections.note: 'mustn't' (prohibition — don't do it) and 'don't have to' (no obligation — your choice) mean very different things. Don't confuse them.

sections.title: First & Second Conditional
sections.rule: The first conditional talks about real, likely future situations: If + present simple, will + base verb. The second conditional talks about unreal or unlikely present/future situations: If + past simple, would + base verb. The past form in the second conditional signals 'imaginary', not past time.
sections.example_target: If it rains, we will stay home.
sections.example_target_2: If I had a million dollars, I would travel the world.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'If it rains, we will stay' = a real possibility for today. / 'If I had a million dollars' = imaginary; I don't have it now.
sections.note: With the verb 'be' in the second conditional, use 'were' for all subjects in careful English: 'If I were you, I would apologize.'

sections.title: Articles: A, An, The
sections.rule: Use 'a/an' for a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time or as one of many ('an' before a vowel sound). Use 'the' when both speaker and listener know which one, or the thing is unique. Use no article for plural or uncountable nouns spoken about in general, and for most proper nouns.
sections.example_target: I saw a dog outside; the dog was barking at a cat.
sections.example_target_2: Dogs are loyal, and the sun is bright today.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: first mention 'a dog', then 'the dog' because now we know which one. / 'Dogs' = dogs in general (no article); 'the sun' = unique.
sections.note: 'a/an' depends on sound, not spelling: 'an hour' (silent h), 'a university' (starts with a 'yoo' sound).

sections.title: Prepositions of Time
sections.rule: Use 'at' for clock times, meals, and fixed points (at 5pm, at night, at Christmas). Use 'in' for longer periods — months, years, seasons, and parts of the day (in July, in 2025, in the morning). Use 'on' for days and dates (on Monday, on May 3rd).
sections.example_target: The meeting is on Monday at 9am in the morning.
sections.example_target_2: I was born in 1990, on a cold day.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'on Monday' (day), 'at 9am' (clock time), 'in the morning' (part of day). / 'in 1990' (year), 'on a cold day' (specific day).
sections.note: Exceptions to memorize: 'at night' (not 'in'), 'at the weekend' (British) vs 'on the weekend' (American).

sections.title: Phrasal Verbs
sections.rule: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle (up, off, out, after) whose combined meaning is often not guessable from the parts: 'give up' means quit. Some are separable (turn it off / turn off the light); others are inseparable (look after her, not 'look her after'). Learn each one as a whole unit.
sections.example_target: Please carry on — don't give up, and I'll find out the answer.
sections.example_target_2: She looks after her little brother every day.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'carry on' = continue; 'give up' = quit; 'find out' = discover. / 'looks after' = takes care of.
sections.note: With a pronoun object, separable phrasal verbs must split: say 'turn it off', never 'turn off it'.

sections.title: Past Continuous & Past Perfect
sections.rule: Use the past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) for an action in progress in the past, often interrupted by a shorter action. Use the past perfect (had + past participle) for the earlier of two past events, to make the order clear. Both add depth to a past-simple narrative.
sections.example_target: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
sections.example_target_2: The train had already left before we arrived.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'was sleeping' = the longer background action; 'rang' interrupted it. / 'had left' happened first, then 'arrived' second.
sections.note: Use the past perfect only when the order isn't otherwise obvious — if you say 'first... then...', simple past is enough.

sections.title: Comparatives & Superlatives
sections.rule: For short adjectives add -er / -est (big → bigger → biggest); double a final consonant after a single vowel. For adjectives of two or more syllables use more / most (useful → more useful → most useful). Comparatives take 'than'; superlatives take 'the'.
sections.example_target: This box is bigger than that one, but it is the biggest in the room.
sections.example_target_2: Her idea is more useful than mine and the most creative of all.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'bigger than' compares two; 'the biggest' picks one out of many. / 'more useful than' compares two; 'the most creative' = top of the group.
sections.note: Learn the irregulars: good → better → best, bad → worse → worst, far → further → furthest.

sections.title: The Passive Voice
sections.rule: Form the passive with be (in the right tense) + past participle. Use it when the action or the object matters more than who did it, or when the doer is unknown or obvious. Add 'by + agent' only if that person is important.
sections.example_target: The letter was written by hand, and English is spoken here.
sections.example_target_2: The bridge is being built right now.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: focus is on the letter and the language, not on who acted. / 'is being built' = passive present continuous, action in progress.
sections.note: Only transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) can be made passive. 'Arrive' or 'sleep' have no passive form.

sections.title: Reported Speech
sections.rule: When reporting what someone said, shift the tense one step back: present → past, will → would, can → could. Also change pronouns and time/place words (now → then, here → there, today → that day). No inversion is used in reported questions.
sections.example_target: He said he was tired and asked where I lived.
sections.example_target_2: She told me she would call the next day.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: original 'I am tired' becomes 'he was tired'; 'Where do you live?' becomes 'where I lived'. / 'I will call tomorrow' becomes 'she would call the next day'.
sections.note: Don't backshift facts that are still true: 'She said the earth is round' can stay present. Reported questions use statement word order: 'asked where I lived', not 'where did I live'.

sections.title: Gerunds vs Infinitives
sections.rule: Some verbs are followed by the gerund (verb-ing): enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest. Others are followed by the infinitive (to + verb): want, decide, hope, promise, need. After every preposition, always use the gerund.
sections.example_target: I enjoy swimming, but I want to rest today.
sections.example_target_2: She is good at cooking and decided to open a restaurant.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'enjoy' takes -ing; 'want' takes to + verb. / 'good at' is a preposition so it takes cooking (-ing); 'decided' takes to open.
sections.note: A few verbs change meaning: 'stop smoking' (quit the habit) vs 'stop to smoke' (pause in order to smoke).

sections.title: Third & Mixed Conditionals
sections.rule: The third conditional imagines a different past: If + past perfect, would have + past participle. It expresses regret or hypothetical past results. Mixed conditionals link a past condition to a present result (would + verb) or a present condition to a past result.
sections.example_target: If I had known, I would have come earlier.
sections.example_target_2: If she had studied medicine, she would be a doctor now.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: I didn't know, so I didn't come — a regret about the past. / A past choice (didn't study medicine) affecting the present (isn't a doctor now).
sections.note: The past perfect ('had known') never means real past here — it is the grammar signal for an imaginary, unreal past.

sections.title: Present Perfect Continuous
sections.rule: Form it with have/has been + verb-ing. It emphasizes the duration of an activity that started in the past and continues to now, or has only just stopped and explains a present result. Use 'for' with a length of time and 'since' with a starting point.
sections.example_target: I have been working all day, so I'm exhausted.
sections.example_target_2: It has been raining since this morning.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'have been working' stresses the ongoing effort and explains why I'm tired. / 'has been raining since' = started this morning and is still going.
sections.note: Prefer the simple present perfect for results/quantity ('I've written three emails') and the continuous for duration ('I've been writing emails').

sections.title: Future Continuous & Perfect
sections.rule: The future continuous (will be + verb-ing) describes an action in progress at a specific future moment. The future perfect (will have + past participle) describes an action that will be completed before a future point. Both let you look forward from a fixed future time.
sections.example_target: At 8pm tonight I will be flying to Tokyo.
sections.example_target_2: By 2030 I will have graduated.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'will be flying' = in progress at 8pm. / 'will have graduated' = finished before the year 2030.
sections.note: The future perfect almost always pairs with 'by' (by then, by next week) to mark the deadline the action beats.

sections.title: Relative Clauses
sections.rule: Defining relative clauses identify which person or thing you mean and take no commas: 'The man who called is here.' Non-defining clauses add extra, optional information and are set off by commas: 'My brother, who lives in Rome, is a chef.' Use who (people), which (things), that (defining only), whose (possession), where (places).
sections.example_target: The book that you lent me was excellent.
sections.example_target_2: Paris, which I visited last year, is beautiful.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'that you lent me' tells us which book (defining, no commas). / 'which I visited last year' is extra detail about Paris (non-defining, commas).
sections.note: You can drop the relative pronoun when it is the object: 'The book you lent me' is fine. Never use 'that' in a non-defining (comma) clause.

sections.title: Used To, Would, Be Used To
sections.rule: 'Used to + base verb' describes past habits and states that are no longer true. 'Would + base verb' also describes repeated past actions, but not past states. 'Be/get used to + noun or verb-ing' means to be (or become) accustomed to something.
sections.example_target: I used to smoke, and we would play outside every summer.
sections.example_target_2: I'm used to waking up early now.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'used to smoke' = a past habit that stopped; 'would play' = a repeated past action. / 'used to waking up early' = I'm accustomed to it (a familiar routine).
sections.note: 'used to do' (past habit) vs 'be used to doing' (accustomed to) look similar but differ completely — watch the 'be' and the -ing.

sections.title: Question Tags
sections.rule: Add a short tag to a statement to invite agreement: statement + reversed auxiliary + pronoun. A positive statement takes a negative tag and vice versa. If the statement has no auxiliary, use do/does/did.
sections.example_target: You're coming, aren't you?
sections.example_target_2: She doesn't drive, does she?
sections.example_ref: Meaning: positive statement 'You're coming' takes the negative tag 'aren't you?'. / negative statement 'She doesn't drive' takes the positive tag 'does she?'.
sections.note: 'I am' takes the irregular tag 'aren't I?', and 'Let's go' takes 'shall we?'. Falling intonation expects agreement; rising intonation is a real question.

sections.title: Causative Have & Get
sections.rule: Use have/get + object + past participle to show that you arranged for someone else to do something for you. The subject does not do the work personally. 'Get' is slightly more informal than 'have'.
sections.example_target: I had my hair cut yesterday.
sections.example_target_2: We are getting the car repaired this week.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: a hairdresser cut my hair — I arranged it, I didn't do it. / a mechanic is repairing the car for us.
sections.note: 'I cut my hair' means you did it yourself; 'I had my hair cut' means a professional did it. The past participle position is essential.

sections.title: Wish & If Only
sections.rule: Use 'wish/if only + past simple' for a present situation you want to be different. Use 'wish + past perfect' for a regret about the past. Use 'wish + would' to complain about an annoying habit or ask for a change.
sections.example_target: I wish I knew the answer.
sections.example_target_2: I wish I had studied harder, and I wish you would stop shouting.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'wish I knew' = I don't know it now, and I want to. / 'wish I had studied' = a past regret; 'wish you would stop' = a complaint about now.
sections.note: After 'wish', use 'were' for all subjects in formal English: 'I wish I were taller.' 'Wish + would' cannot refer to yourself.

sections.title: Past Modals of Deduction
sections.rule: To guess about the past, use modal + have + past participle. 'Must have' shows near certainty, 'can't have' / 'couldn't have' shows it was impossible, and 'might/may/could have' shows possibility. The modal never changes form; only 'have + participle' carries the past meaning.
sections.example_target: She must have left already — her coat is gone.
sections.example_target_2: He can't have known, or he would have warned us.
sections.example_ref: Meaning: 'must have left' = I'm almost sure she left (evidence: the coat). / 'can't have known' = it's impossible that he knew.
sections.note: Use 'can't have' (not 'mustn't have') for a past impossibility. 'mustn't' expresses prohibition, not deduction.
